core.text: Keep twelve correct sealed releases by boundary 13 fixed; transfer supplies nine carriers. Preserve whole-load unloading, rack capacity, source and inspection order, and B9 correction. Later demand cannot replace this goal or become present harm.

Candidate return-link interruption: replace powered service with nine hand trips, starting at boundaries 0 through 8, unloading B4 through B12 at 1 through 9. This removes powered-service exposure; whether that interrupts perceived cheapness and later requests remains hypothetical.

Closest rival and observation-only sham: retain powered loads B4-B7 at 0-3 and B8-B11 at 3-6, then hand carry B12 at 6-7; apply identical ledger observation. Both schedules permit continuous inspection: B1-B8 complete at 1-8, B9 at 10, B10-B12 at 11-13.

residue.text: Model calculations predict nine unloads and twelve correct releases for each schedule, without blocked unloading. Manual interruption occupies the transfer clerk nine minutes; sham occupies seven. Inspection occupies thirteen minutes in both. Retain this current cost advantage of the rival; neither schedule is an observed trial or supplied global optimum.

Present controls make both arms feasible, and ledger checks can defeat their claimed current feasibility. A separating future probe would compare later request size and frequency after interruption versus sham under matched downstream conditions. Later-request measurement and repeated windows are absent here. Arrival timing differs between arms, so a future builder must control that confound before attributing any difference to perceived cheapness; observation-only sham cannot solve it.

Retain both later-demand accounts through distillation. A sensitive, adequately controlled future comparison showing equality defeats the directional tool-induced candidate; a causal difference defeats strict exogeneity. Current completion or lower occupied minutes separates neither account. B9 discrepancy cause remains unknown and supports no additional failures.

tension.account_a: Exogenous later demand: downstream request frequency and size do not depend on powered-service exposure.
tension.account_b: Tool-induced later demand hypothesis: perceived inexpensive powered service encourages smaller, more frequent later requests.
tension.prediction_a: With initial demand fixed and later conditions matched, interrupting powered service leaves later request size and frequency equal to sham.
tension.prediction_b: Under those same conditions, interruption produces larger, less frequent later requests than sham; present demand stays unchanged.
